_meta.description: Canonical GPU, system RAM, and NVMe storage reference for InsiderLLM pipeline. Verified specs are ground truth — models may add to but never contradict these values.
notes: used_price_usd: manually updated from eBay sold listings

used_price_status: 'verified' = firsthand sold-listing data on the stated date; these are the only cards whose age is allowed to go stale (morning-brief §8 nags past 60d). 'researched' = figure from a cited third-party source, believed but not confirmed firsthand; reported as an informational count, never nagged on age. 'unverified' = no defensible band (mid-only or never priced); never fill these by inference. See used_price_note for per-card reasoning.

2026-07-25 refresh: rtx-3090-24gb and rtx-3060-12gb re-priced from firsthand eBay sold listings, superseding May/March research figures. The other cards were NOT touched — no firsthand data existed for them, and a stale-but-honest number beats a fabricated fresh one. morning-brief.py §8 reports their age daily.
benchmarks: manually verified from trusted sources
specs: cross-referenced against techpowerup.com GPU database
bandwidth predicts tok/s for memory-bound LLM inference
VRAM is the primary constraint for model size that fits on GPU
May 2026 refresh: RTX 3090 appreciating due to local AI demand (used median ~$1,000, premium AIB $1,100-1,300)
DRAM shortage affecting 16GB+ Blackwell cards (RTX 5070 Ti, RTX 5060 Ti 16GB) — street prices inflated above MSRP
tier field added (entry/mid/high/flagship) for Hugo shortcode filtering
ebay_sold_url field added for one-click sold-listing access during quarterly updates

2026-07-27: used_price_status normalized to a three-value enum (verified/researched/unverified) and per-card prose moved to used_price_note. rx-7800-xt-16gb re-priced from firsthand eBay sold listings ($400-465-550), superseding the March research figure.
2026-07-27: rtx-4090-24gb re-priced from firsthand eBay sold listings ($2,100-2,250-2,550), superseding the May 2026 research figure of $2,200-2,400-2,600. Fourth verified card.

2026-08-04: added `storage` — 2TB NVMe price bands from firsthand eBay sold listings, keyed by host interface generation following the system_ram precedent. storage._host_interface_rule is BOARD-CONDITIONAL and carries an explicit quotation_warning; it is false if quoted without the PCIe 3.0 host condition. No consumer reads `storage` — GPU_PROSE_CARDS was deliberately not extended, so the drift checker does not scan storage prices.

listed_price_* vs used_price_*: TWO DIFFERENT CLASSES OF EVIDENCE, never interchangeable. used_price_usd with used_price_status='verified' is firsthand SOLD data — what buyers actually paid — and is the ground truth the drift checker and the prose rules are built on. listed_price_usd is firsthand ACTIVE-LISTING asks — what sellers want, which no buyer has agreed to. A card carrying listed_price_usd and no used_price_usd has NOT been priced in the sense the rest of this file means. Do not promote a listed band into a sold band, do not average the two, and do not let a listed figure satisfy a rule that asks for a verified price.

2026-08-10: Intel Arc Pro series added (B70 32GB, B60 24GB, B60 Dual 48GB, B50 16GB) — the first Intel entries and the first cards in this file priced from listed asks rather than sold listings. All four carry used_price_status='unverified' with null used_price_usd, deliberately, so the sold-price machinery treats them as unpriced. Specs are verified: each bandwidth figure was checked by arithmetic against bus width and memory clock (B70 256-bit x 19 Gbps = 608, B60 192-bit x 19 = 456, B50 128-bit x 14 = 224) rather than taken from a spec-sheet summary. Three release dates left null rather than guessed.

arc-pro-b60-dual-48gb records PER-GPU bandwidth and bus width against a BOARD-TOTAL vram_gb, because it is two 24GB devices on one card. Any consumer of this file that assumes vram_gb is one addressable pool will size models wrong on that entry, and only that entry.

2026-08-18: rtx-5090-32gb re-priced from firsthand eBay sold listings (n=89 single cards over 2026-08-08..08-18; used band $3,900/$4,220/$4,400 p25/median/p75), superseding the 2026-07-31 figures. MSRP re-verified at $1,999 against NVIDIA's own CES launch release, not a secondary source. Band is stated as an interquartile range and the note says so, because the full min-max included two sub-$2,700 listings that are almost certainly mislistings. rules.msrp_vs_street instance updated to match.

2026-08-19: rtx-3090-24gb re-priced from firsthand eBay sold listings (n=68 single cards — 52 used/open-box, 16 eBay Refurbished), superseding the 2026-07-25 band of $1,000/$1,200/$1,400. New band $1,200/$1,300/$1,400. The old $1,000 low was unreachable: nothing sold below $1,099. Banded on the POOLED used-plus-refurbished market rather than the used subset, because the 3090 is EOL and has no new tier — the 5090's used-only convention exists to separate new from used and does not apply here. The pooled IQR was not used directly: the distribution is bimodal and its IQR falls between the two modes. See used_price_note. Fifth verified card. rtx-3090-ti-24gb was NOT touched — it is a different card, still 'researched' from bestvaluegpu.com May 2026, and wants its own pull.

2026-08-19: added rules.as_purchased_is_history_not_market. As-purchased costs in firsthand narratives are historical facts, not market claims, and the drift check cannot tell them apart from stale prices. The fix is a DATE LABEL, not a skip term — see the rule's do_not field, and note its cross_reference to invariant (v), whose proposed fix would break this convention unless purchase-tense verbs are added to the historical pattern.

gtx-1660-super.name: NVIDIA GTX 1660 Super
gtx-1660-super.ai_notes: 6GB VRAM limits to 7B quantized models. No tensor cores. Fine for experimentation, not for daily use.

rtx-2060-12gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 2060 12GB
rtx-2060-12gb.ai_notes: 12GB VRAM is great, but bandwidth matches GTX 1660 Super. Tensor cores help with some workloads. Decent budget option if found cheap.

rtx-3060-12gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 3060 12GB
rtx-3060-12gb.ai_notes: The entry-level workhorse. 12GB fits 13B Q4 models. Bandwidth is the bottleneck — half the 3080's speed. Still the cheapest honest 12GB, though the 2026 memory shortage lifted the floor off ~$170.

qwen35_9b_think_on.notes: Ollama qwen3.5:9b think=true, 4x token overhead (871→3404 tokens)

deepseek_r1_14b_think_on.notes: Ollama deepseek-r1:14b think=true, 3x token overhead (380→921 tokens)

rtx-3060-ti-8gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 3060 Ti
rtx-3060-ti-8gb.ai_notes: Faster than the 3060 12GB at gaming and 25% more bandwidth, but 8GB caps it at 7B-class models. The used market now prices it BELOW the 3060 12GB despite the higher tier badge — VRAM, not gaming performance, sets the price. Same $/GB as the 3060 12GB with a third less memory.
rtx-3060-ti-8gb.used_price_note: Working cards; bulk of sales $190-230. Excluded: parts-only ($50-132), Canada-based auctions ($163-172, currency), and a $555 Yeston outlier.

rtx-3070-8gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 3070
rtx-3070-8gb.ai_notes: Fast but 8GB VRAM is limiting. Only fits 7B Q4 comfortably. Higher bandwidth than 3060 but less VRAM makes it a tradeoff.

rtx-3070-ti-8gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 3070 Ti
rtx-3070-ti-8gb.ai_notes: GDDR6X gives much better bandwidth than 3070. Still 8GB VRAM limited. Power hungry for what you get.

rtx-3080-10gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 3080 10GB
rtx-3080-10gb.ai_notes: 2x the bandwidth of 3060. 10GB fits 7B Q4 and some 13B Q2. The speed upgrade is dramatic if models fit in VRAM.

rtx-3080-12gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 3080 12GB
rtx-3080-12gb.ai_notes: The sleeper pick. 12GB VRAM + 912 GB/s bandwidth = 3060's model capacity at 2.5x the speed. Hard to find but excellent value.

llama3_8b_q4.notes: 3080 Ti proxy — same GA102, same bandwidth; llama.cpp CUDA tg1024

rtx-3090-24gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 3090
rtx-3090-24gb.ai_notes: 24GB at 936 GB/s. Best price-per-VRAM-GB for 24GB, but appreciating through 2026 as local AI demand outruns gaming depreciation. Pooled used/refurbished median ~$1,300 (2026-08-19); nothing sold below $1,099, so there is no sub-$1,100 3090.

gemma3_27b.notes: Ollama gemma3:27b, RTX 3090 24GB. 27B model fits entirely in VRAM.

rtx-3090-24gb.used_price_note: Pulled 2026-08-19 from eBay SOLD + completed, Buy It Now, US only, single cards. n=68: 52 used/open-box, 16 eBay Refurbished. Used subset p25/median/p75 = $1,200 / $1,275 / $1,300 (range $1,099-1,420); refurbished $1,399 / $1,400 / $1,494 (range $1,300-1,800); all 68 pooled $1,249 / $1,300 / $1,374 (range $1,099-1,800). BAND IS THE POOLED USED-PLUS-REFURBISHED MARKET, not the used subset alone — unlike the 5090 there is no new tier to separate out. The card is EOL, every unit a buyer can get is secondhand, and eBay Refurbished is a seller grade inside that same market rather than a distinct product, so both grades come back in one search. THE POOLED IQR ITSELF WAS NOT USED as the band: the distribution is bimodal (used mode ~$1,275, refurbished mode ~$1,400) and the pooled IQR of $1,249-$1,374 falls in the valley between them, excluding the entire refurbished mode. Band is therefore used p25 ($1,200) to refurbished median ($1,400) with the pooled median ($1,300) as mid, which covers both modes. The refurbished upper tail ($1,400-1,800) sits ABOVE the band by design — a page quoting $1,500+ should flag and be checked, not auto-accepted. THE $1,000 FLOOR WAS UNREACHABLE: nothing sold below $1,099 across 52 used cards, so the previous low was $100 under the cheapest real sale and roughly $200 under the used p25. Supersedes the 2026-07-25 band ($1,000/$1,200/$1,400). The median moved +8.3% ($1,200 -> $1,300) in 25 days while the high held, so the band tightened and shifted up. Spread is $200 against the 5090's $500 on a comparable IQR — a settled market, not a constrained one. Excluded: 3090 Ti, 4090, 7900 XTX, Quadro/workstation variants, parts-only, multi-card bundles, and one broken-fan card.

rtx-4060-8gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 4060
rtx-4060-8gb.ai_notes: Lowest bandwidth of any current card. 8GB VRAM and 128-bit bus make it worse than an RTX 3060 12GB for AI despite being newer. Avoid for local AI.

llama3_8b_q4.notes: localscore community median; may include laptop variants

rtx-4060-ti-8gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti 8GB
rtx-4060-ti-8gb.ai_notes: Same 128-bit bus problem as 4060. More compute but still bandwidth-starved for LLM inference. The 16GB version is much better.

rtx-4060-ti-16gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti 16GB
rtx-4060-ti-16gb.ai_notes: 16GB VRAM is great for model capacity but 128-bit bus caps bandwidth at 288 GB/s. Runs bigger models than 3060 but slower token generation. Trade VRAM for speed vs the 3080 12GB.

rx-7600-8gb.name: AMD Radeon RX 7600
rx-7600-8gb.ai_notes: ROCm support improving but still behind CUDA. 8GB VRAM and 128-bit bus limit AI use. Only consider if you specifically want AMD and accept the software tradeoffs.

rx-7700-xt-12gb.name: AMD Radeon RX 7700 XT
rx-7700-xt-12gb.ai_notes: 12GB VRAM with better bandwidth than RTX 3060. ROCm compatibility is the main risk. If AMD software works for your stack, this is competitive.

rx-7800-xt-16gb.name: AMD Radeon RX 7800 XT
rx-7800-xt-16gb.ai_notes: 16GB VRAM + 624 GB/s bandwidth makes this AMD's best AI value if ROCm works for you. Competes with RTX 3080 12GB in bandwidth territory.
rx-7800-xt-16gb.used_price_note: Working cards only; thickest band $440-490, premium AIBs and refurbs $500-550. Excluded from the range: parts-only listings ($125-280), bundles, and three scam listings at $44.99. New retail runs $600-700, so the used-vs-new spread is unusually thin - memory-shortage compression is holding new prices down toward used.

rx-7900-gre-16gb.name: AMD Radeon RX 7900 GRE
rx-7900-gre-16gb.ai_notes: Navi 31 chip means more compute units than 7800 XT but slightly lower bandwidth. 16GB VRAM. ROCm compatibility varies — test before committing.

rx-7900-xt-20gb.name: AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT
rx-7900-xt-20gb.ai_notes: 20GB VRAM is between 3090 and 4060 Ti 16GB in capacity. 800 GB/s bandwidth is competitive. AMD's best current option for local AI if ROCm support works.

rtx-5060.name: NVIDIA RTX 5060
rtx-5060.ai_notes: PRELIMINARY — specs not confirmed. Likely 8GB VRAM with 128-bit bus. If so, same VRAM limitation as RTX 4060.

rtx-5060-ti.name: NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti
rtx-5060-ti.ai_notes: PRELIMINARY — specs not confirmed. 16GB GDDR7 rumored. If bandwidth improves over 4060 Ti 16GB, could be a solid mid-range AI card.

rtx-5070.name: NVIDIA RTX 5070
rtx-5070.ai_notes: GDDR7 gives 672 GB/s on a 192-bit bus — impressive. 12GB VRAM same as 3060 but nearly 2x bandwidth. Availability and actual pricing TBD.

rx-9070.name: AMD Radeon RX 9070
rx-9070.ai_notes: PRELIMINARY — 16GB VRAM with 256-bit bus. ROCm support status for RDNA 4 unknown. Wait for confirmed local AI benchmarks before recommending.
rx-9070.used_price_note: Never priced. RDNA 4 used market is thin and we have no firsthand sold-listing data; left null deliberately rather than guessed.

rx-9070-xt.name: AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT
rx-9070-xt.ai_notes: PRELIMINARY — same memory subsystem as RX 9070. More compute units. Same ROCm uncertainty as 9070.

rtx-3090-ti-24gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti
rtx-3090-ti-24gb.ai_notes: Slightly faster than 3090 (~10-15%) with same 24GB. NVLink removed vs vanilla 3090 — less attractive for dual-card AI setups. Higher power draw (450W vs 350W). Used/open-box median $1,400 (2026-09-02), a $100 premium over the vanilla 3090's $1,300 measured in the same pull.
rtx-3090-ti-24gb.used_price_note: Pulled 2026-09-02 from eBay SOLD + completed, Buy It Now, US only, single cards, window ~2026-08-23 to 09-02 (pages 1-2 of sold listings). n=46: 41 used/open-box, 5 eBay Refurbished. Used subset p25/median/p75 = $1,300 / $1,400 / $1,499 (range $1,100-1,750); refurbished $1,469 / $1,499 / $1,589 (range $1,449-1,599). FILTERED ON "Ti" IN THE TITLE, NOT eBay's CHIPSET FIELD, which is seller-entered and is wrong for this card constantly. Some sellers omit "Ti" from the title, so this sample UNDER-counts rather than over-counts — the direction of the error is known and is the safe one. BAND FOLLOWS THE 2026-08-19 VANILLA 3090 METHOD: used p25 as the low, and a high that two independent statistics agree on — used p75 and the refurbished median are BOTH $1,499. That agreement is what carries the high, because n=5 refurbished is far too small for its median to bound anything on its own. Mid is the USED median, not a pooled median: the pooled figure was not computed in this pull, and with refurbished at 11% of the sample it would sit between $1,400 and roughly $1,440 — stated as a range rather than written into the field, because an estimate does not belong in a verified entry. MEDIAN IS STABLE ACROSS SAMPLE SIZE: $1,400 on page 1 alone (n=19) and $1,400 again at n=41. The used upper tail ($1,500-1,750) sits ABOVE the band by design, as on the vanilla card — a page quoting $1,500+ should flag and be checked, not auto-accepted. SUPERSEDES the 2026-05-18 bestvaluegpu.com researched figure ($1,150 / $1,199 / $1,400), which was low by $150 at the floor and by $200 at the mid. That entry was a cited third-party figure; this one is firsthand sold data on the same method as the vanilla 3090. PREMIUM OVER THE VANILLA CARD, measured in the same pull: vanilla n=88, p25/median/p75 = $1,200 / $1,300 / $1,400, so the Ti premium is exactly $100 at the median. Excluded: vanilla 3090s, 4090, parts-only, multi-card bundles.

rtx-4070-12gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 4070
rtx-4070-12gb.ai_notes: 12GB VRAM, decent bandwidth, very efficient (200W). Fits 14B Q4 comfortably. RTX 4070 Super is the better buy if you can find one.

rtx-4070-ti-super-16gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti Super
rtx-4070-ti-super-16gb.ai_notes: 16GB at 672 GB/s makes this a solid AI card for 30B-class models. Better value than 4080 in many cases.
rtx-4070-ti-super-16gb.used_price_note: Working cards; bulk of sales $700-800. Excluded: parts-only ($139-520), China-based new listings ($1,098-1,499), and a STALKER special edition at $1,150.

rtx-4080-16gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 4080
rtx-4080-16gb.ai_notes: 16GB GDDR6X, solid bandwidth. Superseded by 4080 SUPER on price/perf. For AI, 4070 Ti Super at $799 is often the better buy unless found cheap used.

rtx-4090-24gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 4090
rtx-4090-24gb.ai_notes: 24GB, 1008 GB/s, FP8 support. Fastest 24GB consumer card. Used market data conflicted as of 2026-05-18 — verify before populating prices.
rtx-4090-24gb.used_price_note: Working cards only, ~16 clean listings clustering $2,100-2,250. Excluded: parts-only ($98-1,950), a $1,600 waterblock bundle, and a $1,425 parts-only that drew 30 bids.

rtx-5070-ti-16gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti
rtx-5070-ti-16gb.ai_notes: $749 MSRP, but street prices $850-1,000+ due to 16GB GDDR7 supply constraints (DRAM shortage). RTX 5070 Ti SUPER (24GB) rumored October 2026 — buyers may want to wait.
rtx-5070-ti-16gb.used_price_source: bestvaluegpu.com May 2026 — inflated above $749 MSRP due to DRAM shortage
rtx-5070-ti-16gb.used_price_note: Mid only, no low/high band. bestvaluegpu.com May 2026 figure is inflated above the $749 MSRP by the DRAM shortage.

rtx-5080-16gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 5080
rtx-5080-16gb.ai_notes: 16GB GDDR7. EOL rumored October 2026 in favor of RTX 5080 SUPER (24GB) — buyers may want to wait.
rtx-5080-16gb.used_price_note: Mid only, no low/high band established.

rtx-5090-32gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 5090
rtx-5090-32gb.ai_notes: 32GB flagship with NVFP4 support, 1792 GB/s bandwidth. Ongoing supply constraints since launch - street sits at roughly 2.1x the $1,999 MSRP (used median $4,220, 2026-08-18) and the card is not sustainably available at MSRP from any major retailer.
rtx-5090-32gb.used_price_note: Pulled 2026-08-18 from eBay SOLD + completed, Buy It Now, US only, _sacat=27386, window 2026-08-08 to 2026-08-18. n=89 single cards: 61 used/open-box/refurb, 28 new/sealed. Band is the USED subset stated as p25 / median / p75 = $3,900 / $4,220 / $4,400, i.e. the interquartile range rather than the full min-max, because two low outliers are not market prices (a $2,600 SUPRIM LIQUID and a $2,150 ROG Astral, both listed Brand New with best offer accepted, read as mislistings or scams). Full used range was $2,868-4,800. New/sealed ran $4,025 / $4,500 / $4,787 (p25/median/p75, range $2,600-8,495); all 89 single cards median $4,250. THE NEW-OVER-USED PREMIUM IS ONLY ~$280, which points at supply constraint rather than a condition premium - on an unconstrained card new sits far above used. Excluded: multi-card lots, parts-only, eGPU units, and one NO CORE listing. Against the verified $1,999 MSRP this is 1.95x-2.20x used (2.11x at the median) and 2.25x at the new median. Supersedes the 2026-07-31 figures ($3,000/$3,800/$4,700); the median moved up and the band tightened considerably. Cross-check on the same date: retail NEW asks sit ABOVE this used median - Amazon $4,598.90 in stock per videocardprices.com, Newegg median ~$4,700 - so the secondary market was the cheaper route, which is the same supply-constraint signal from the other side.

tesla-p40-24gb.name: NVIDIA Tesla P40
tesla-p40-24gb.ai_notes: 24GB at a measured $230 median bare / $288 with cooling (2026-09-02). The card is PASSIVELY COOLED and gets no airflow in a desktop, so the bare price is not the usable price — budget the cooled figure, ~$58 more at the median. But: Pascal arch lost CUDA support in CUDA 13 (Oct 2025). No tensor cores. Vulkan/llama.cpp only now. Skip for new builds.
tesla-p40-24gb.used_price_note: Pulled 2026-09-02 from eBay SOLD + completed, Buy It Now, US only, single cards, window 2026-06-09 to 09-02 (single page, three months of sales). n=78, and it is BIMODAL ON COOLING rather than on seller grade: bare card n=60 pulled, p25/median/p75 = $220 / $230 / $250 (in-window range $199-360; two Feb 2026 stragglers at $190 and $195 excluded — they predate the Jun 9 window, were the sample minima, and do not cross a quartile in the $225-250 cluster); with fan/shroud/adapter n=18, $250 / $288 / $326 (range $240-349). THE COOLING SPLIT IS A FINDING, NOT NOISE, AND THE TWO FIGURES MUST NOT BE COLLAPSED. The P40 is passively cooled and has no fan of its own, so it gets no airflow in an ordinary desktop; a bare card is not a usable card for our readers. The gap is ~$58 at the median. HOW THE SPLIT IS REPRESENTED HERE: low $220 = bare p25, high $288 = cooled median, so the band SPANS BOTH MODES and a page quoting either a bare or a cooled price is accepted without a false flag. Mid $230 is the BARE median — deliberately not an average of the two modes, which would describe no card that actually exists and would be wrong in both directions at once. Bare is 60 of 78 cards (77%), so it is the honest single figure, and the shortcode renders low-mid-high to readers, which is a second reason not to put a synthetic number in it. Carry BOTH figures wherever this card appears in prose. The cooled upper tail ($289-349) sits above the band by design; so does the bare tail to $360. SUPERSEDES the 2026-05-19 researched figure ($190 / $270 / $350). That mid sat between the two modes — above every bare quartile and below the cooled median — which is exactly the collapse this entry avoids. Excluded: a 5-card lot at $895, a 2-card lot at $325, a $1,299.95 P40/P41 mislisting, a $115 AS-IS non-working card, and a $405 "Brand New" outlier.

rtx-2080-ti-22gb.name: NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti 22GB (modded)
rtx-2080-ti-22gb.ai_notes: Chinese-modded variant: 11GB chips swapped for 22GB. Turing arch supports current CUDA. 616 GB/s + 22GB is a credible value play for AI. Not OEM — buy only from sellers with verified mod history.

arc-pro-b70-32gb.name: Intel Arc Pro B70
arc-pro-b70-32gb.ai_notes: 32GB for roughly the price of a used 3090, at 608 GB/s against the 3090's 936 — capacity per dollar is the reason to buy it, bandwidth is the reason not to. Bandwidth confirmed by arithmetic, not just reporting: 256-bit at 19 Gbps = 608 GB/s. llama.cpp reaches this card through the SYCL backend, which is the practical difference against non-CUDA accelerators that have no GGUF path at all. The vLLM path is less settled — StorageReview's March 2026 review calls Intel's vLLM support beta-grade with limited model coverage and quantization paths that should work but do not. Buy on VRAM, expect to troubleshoot.
arc-pro-b70-32gb.used_price_note: No firsthand SOLD-listing data exists for this card. Left null deliberately rather than derived from asking prices. See listed_price_* for active-listing asks, which are what sellers want and not what buyers paid — a weaker class of evidence than every used_price_usd band in this file, and not interchangeable with one.
arc-pro-b70-32gb.listed_price_source: firsthand eBay ACTIVE listings, Graphics/Video Cards category, pulled 2026-08-10 (19 Arc Pro B70 results)
arc-pro-b70-32gb.listed_price_note: US new band. Cheapest US new was $1,361.49 (ASRock), then $1,375.43 and $1,440.50. One US open-box at $1,250 sits below the band and is excluded from it. Non-US and boutique listings ran $1,734-$2,489 and are excluded as implausible against domestic, the same exclusion applied to the RTX 5090 sold data. THESE ARE ASKS. No sale is evidenced at any of these numbers.
arc-pro-b70-32gb.msrp_vs_street_note: $949 MSRP against a $1,360-1,440 US street band — 1.43x to 1.52x MSRP. See rules.msrp_vs_street; this is the second recorded instance of the gap after the RTX 5090.

arc-pro-b60-24gb.name: Intel Arc Pro B60
arc-pro-b60-24gb.ai_notes: 24GB at 456 GB/s (192-bit at 19 Gbps). Matches a 3090 on capacity and gives up roughly half its bandwidth, so it loads what a 3090 loads and decodes slower. Cheapest route to 24GB that is new with a warranty. release_date left null — announced at Computex 2025 and widely reported as shipping September 2025, but no exact date verified firsthand.
arc-pro-b60-24gb.used_price_note: No firsthand SOLD-listing data exists for this card. Left null deliberately rather than derived from asking prices. See listed_price_* for active-listing asks, which are what sellers want and not what buyers paid — a weaker class of evidence than every used_price_usd band in this file, and not interchangeable with one.
arc-pro-b60-24gb.listed_price_source: firsthand eBay ACTIVE listings, Graphics/Video Cards category, pulled 2026-08-10 (19 Arc Pro B70 results)
arc-pro-b60-24gb.listed_price_note: US new band from two listings: $744.14 (ARKN, free shipping, 21 watchers) and $792.68 (ASRock B60CT24G). A $929 listing shipping from China is excluded as non-US. Two observations is a thin basis for a band — treat as indicative. THESE ARE ASKS, not sales.
arc-pro-b60-24gb.msrp_vs_street_note: $599 MSRP against $744-793 asks — 1.24x to 1.32x MSRP. Same direction as the B70 and smaller. See rules.msrp_vs_street.

arc-pro-b60-dual-48gb.name: Intel Arc Pro B60 Dual 48GB
arc-pro-b60-dual-48gb.ai_notes: READ THE MEMORY FIELDS CAREFULLY. This is two B60 GPUs on one board, not one 48GB device. vram_gb is the board total; bus_width_bit and bandwidth_gbs are PER GPU, because that is what a model actually sees. A 48GB model does not fit — it must be split across two 24GB devices, with the split traffic crossing PCIe. Anything that treats 48GB as one pool will size models wrong. MSRP is the Maxsun Dual 48G Turbo at $1,200. Power left null; no verified TBP.

arc-pro-b50-16gb.ai_notes: 16GB at 224 GB/s (128-bit at 14 Gbps) on 70W with no external power connector, so it drops into a small-form-factor box that cannot take anything else. Bandwidth is the constraint: 224 GB/s is a quarter of a 3090's, so it holds a 30B at Q3 and decodes it slowly. Announced at $299 at Computex 2025 and launched at $349; msrp_usd carries the launch figure, not the announcement.

ddr3.ai_notes: 12.8 GB/s dual-channel max. CPU offloading at 3-4x slower than DDR5. Fine for models that fit entirely in VRAM. Painful for offloaded layers.

ddr4.ai_notes: 25.6 GB/s at 3200MHz dual-channel. 2x DDR3 performance for offloading. Sweet spot for budget builds — Optiplex 5060/7060 are cheap and take DDR4.

ddr5.ai_notes: 48 GB/s at 6000MHz dual-channel. 4x DDR3 for offloading. Best for CPU-heavy workloads or large models that need lots of offloaded layers. Premium cost.

_meta.description: NVMe SSD pricing and interface reference. Bands are for 2TB M.2 NVMe, the capacity where local-AI model storage actually gets decided.
_meta.price_basis_note: Firsthand sold-listing data, same method and standard as used_price_status='verified' on the GPU entries.

market_conditions.summary: 2026 NVMe pricing is elevated against historical norms.
market_conditions.cause: NAND and DRAM market pressure — the same supply dynamic driving the 2026 GPU and system-RAM pricing recorded elsewhere in this file.
market_conditions.implication: Do not treat these bands as a long-run floor. A 2TB drive at these prices is expensive by pre-2026 standards, and the $/GB comparisons against older articles will not line up.

nvme_gen3.ai_notes: The correct buy for a PCIe 3.0 host. Model load is a large sequential read, so sustained throughput matters more than random IOPS — prefer TLC with a DRAM cache over DRAM-less at the same price. A 13-rung -ncmoe sweep reloads the weights once per rung, which is where load speed shows up.

nvme_gen4.ai_notes: Only worth the premium on a PCIe 4.0 host — see _host_interface_rule. Note that budget Gen4 drives are often rated at or near the Gen3 ceiling anyway (the Patriot P400 Lite peaks at 3,500 MB/s), so 'Gen4' on the box does not by itself mean faster than Gen3.

_host_interface_rule.claim: A Gen4 NVMe delivers no sequential-throughput advantage over a Gen3 NVMe.
_host_interface_rule.holds_only_when: the host board's M.2 slot is PCIe 3.0
_host_interface_rule.does_not_hold_when: the host board's M.2 slot is PCIe 4.0 or newer, where a Gen4 drive can exceed the Gen3 ceiling
_host_interface_rule.mechanism: The PCIe 3.0 x4 host link caps at roughly 3,500 MB/s. Both generations saturate that same ceiling, so the drive's own higher rating is unreachable.
_host_interface_rule.buying_implication_when_it_holds: Buy Gen3. The Gen4 price premium purchases throughput the board cannot deliver.
_host_interface_rule.quotation_warning: BOARD-CONDITIONAL. Quoting this claim without the PCIe 3.0 host condition makes it false. On a Gen4 board the premium is spendable.

_sold_examples.dram_cache_note: not stated in the sold-listing data; left null rather than inferred

_sold_examples.note: Low end of the Gen3 band. TLC with DRAM at this price is the value case for a PCIe 3.0 host.

_sold_examples.rated_note: Rated peak equals the PCIe 3.0 host ceiling, so this Gen4 drive would not beat Gen3 sequential even on a Gen4 board. Interface generation and rated speed verified from vendor and retailer specs, not from the sold listing.

rules.bandwidth_impact: For models that fit entirely in VRAM, memory bandwidth is the primary predictor of tok/s. Double the bandwidth ≈ double the tok/s for memory-bound inference.
rules.offload_penalty: Each layer offloaded to CPU RAM runs at system RAM bandwidth instead of VRAM bandwidth. DDR4-3200 (25.6 GB/s) vs GDDR6X (936 GB/s) = ~37x slower per offloaded layer.
rules.power_budget: Budget builds often reuse old PSUs. Cards over 250W TDP need PSU upgrade. Factor $40-80 for a used 750W PSU.
rules.rocm_caveat: AMD ROCm support is improving but not all models/frameworks work. Always verify ROCm compatibility for your specific use case before buying AMD for AI.

msrp_vs_street.claim: MSRP is not what a buyer pays. On supply-constrained or recently launched cards it can sit far below street, and quoting it next to another card's street price compares two different kinds of number.
msrp_vs_street.mechanism: MSRP is the vendor's launch figure and never moves. Street is set by the market and moves with supply. Where the two diverge, a comparison built on MSRP understates the buy-in by whatever the gap is.

instances.street_basis: firsthand eBay SOLD listings, used subset p25-p75, n=61
firsthand eBay ACTIVE listings — asks, not sales

msrp_vs_street.editorial_rule: Label every price with what it is. Write 'MSRP' when that is all you have, and never present it as the buy-in. When both are known, lead with street.
msrp_vs_street.cross_reference: dated-markers.md 2026-08-14, '5090 MSRP-vs-street editorial sweep'. The B70 is the second recorded instance and it is neither NVIDIA-specific nor scarcity-specific — one is an anecdote, two across different vendors and different causes is the case for a house convention rather than per-card notes. All four Arc Pro cards show the gap in the same direction, which makes it five instances if the thin-evidence three are counted.
msrp_vs_street.occasion: Newsletter #17 (2026-08-10) cited the B70 at its $949 MSRP against the Tenstorrent p150a's $1,399 street price, which made Intel read as cheaper when it is the same money. Corrected in commit 2af9478 before the blog page was built.

as_purchased_is_history_not_market.claim: A price someone actually paid, in a firsthand narrative, is a fact about a transaction, not a claim about the current market. It never goes stale — it is simply about a different date.
as_purchased_is_history_not_market.mechanism: The drift check compares every money figure near a card name against the current store band. It cannot tell 'this is what the market is' from 'this is what I paid'. Repricing an as-purchased figure falsifies the account, and where several sum to a stated total, repricing one breaks the arithmetic of the piece as well.
as_purchased_is_history_not_market.editorial_rule: Label the date wherever the figure stands without narrative tense to carry it. Past-tense prose ('the card cost $850') already reads as history; a bare figure in a table cell or a quick_answer does not. Label once per block — a table header ('Cost paid (early 2026)') covers every row under it.
as_purchased_is_history_not_market.do_not: Do NOT add a GPU_PRICE_SKIP_ term for this shape. A skip term silences the figure for the checker and leaves the READER with an unlabelled number that looks stale, which is the wrong half of the problem. The label fixes both halves — and a correctly worded label already satisfies GPU_PRICE_SKIP_HISTORICAL on its own merits, because the figure genuinely is historical.
